final_review.summary: The paper proposes AEMC-NE, an autoencoder-based matrix completion method augmented with a shared element-wise neural network that learns an adaptive output activation. The idea is technically plausible and useful, and the paper combines it with MCAR and MNAR generalization analyses plus broad empirical evaluation across synthetic, collaborative filtering, ranking, runtime, and imputation settings. However, the central modeling contribution is incremental relative to prior nonlinear decoder and adaptive activation work, and the empirical evidence has important weaknesses: limited statistical reporting, unclear baseline comparability, and insufficient capacity-matched ablations on the main benchmarks. The theoretical bounds are relevant but mostly qualitative and depend on assumptions that are not fully validated in practice. Overall, the work is promising and generally well presented, but the current evidence does not quite support acceptance at ICLR.

strengths.item: Introduces a simple, parameter-efficient extension to autoencoder matrix completion by learning a shared element-wise output nonlinearity.
Provides theoretical analysis under both MCAR and MNAR missingness settings, including an appendix extension for estimated propensities.
Reports a broad empirical evaluation across synthetic data, MovieLens, Douban, Flixster, ranking metrics, runtime analyses, and UCI imputation tasks.
The method is easy to understand, technically plausible, and consistently improves over standard AEMC or AutoRec-style baselines in the reported experiments.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear equations, theorem statements, and informative tables and captions.

weaknesses.item: The core architectural novelty is moderate, since the element-wise network can be interpreted as a constrained nonlinear decoder or adaptive activation function.
The empirical results are mostly single point estimates without repeated runs, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests.
Baseline comparability is unclear because many results appear to be literature numbers rather than reruns under identical splits, preprocessing, validation, and tuning protocols.
The main experiments do not sufficiently isolate the benefit of the element-wise module from added model capacity or decoder depth using parameter-matched autoencoder baselines.

The theoretical guarantees rely on strong assumptions, including MCAR sampling or accurate positive propensities, boundedness, Lipschitzness, and capacity constraints that are only partially connected to the implementation.
The approach has practical scope limitations, including difficulty adapting to new users and no treatment of cold-start settings.

requested_changes.item: Add repeated-run results with standard deviations or confidence intervals, and include statistical significance tests for the main benchmark comparisons.
Clarify which baselines were rerun versus taken from prior work, and ensure fair comparison under shared data splits, preprocessing, validation, and hyperparameter tuning.
Include stronger capacity-matched and depth-matched autoencoder ablations on the primary collaborative filtering benchmarks to isolate the contribution of the shared element-wise network.
Better connect the assumptions in the generalization bounds to the actual training procedure and empirical settings, especially for real MNAR recommendation data where true propensities are unknown.
Improve readability of dense theoretical sections and enlarge small visual elements in figures.
